content: Febrile neutropenia is a common and potentially life-threatening complication in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. The standard treatment for this condition involves supportive care combined with antibiotics. Colony-stimulating factors (CSFs), such as granulocyte-CSF (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage CSF (GM-CSF), are cytokines that promote the production and maturation of specific blood cell lines in the bone marrow. Clinical trials have investigated whether adding CSFs to antibiotics could improve outcomes in patients with febrile neutropenia, but the results of these studies have been inconsistent. The objective of this review was to assess the safety and efficacy of adding G-CSF or GM-CSF to standard antibiotic therapy in the treatment of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia in cancer patients. A comprehensive search of major electronic databases was conducted in March 2014, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and SCI. Additional searches for economic evaluations were performed in May 2015. Experts in hematology and oncology were consulted, and references from relevant articles were reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and economic evaluations comparing CSF plus antibiotics versus antibiotics alone were included. Fourteen RCTs, encompassing 15 comparisons and a total of 1,553 participants, were included in the analysis. The addition of CSFs to antibiotics did not significantly improve overall mortality compared to antibiotics alone (hazard ratio [HR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 1.16, P = 0.19; low-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant improvement was observed in infection-related mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.20, P = 0.23; low-quality evidence). However, patients receiving CSFs in addition to antibiotics were less likely to experience hospital stays exceeding 10 days (risk ratio [RR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95, P = 0.03; low-quality evidence). They also demonstrated faster recovery of neutrophil counts (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.81, P = 0.004; moderate-quality evidence) compared to those treated with antibiotics alone. Furthermore, the duration of neutropenia was shorter in the CSF group (standardized mean difference [SMD] -1.70, 95% CI -2.65 to -0.76, P = 0.0004; moderate-quality evidence), as was the time to fever resolution (SMD -0.49, 95% CI -0.90 to -0.09, P = 0.02; moderate-quality evidence) and the duration of antibiotic use (SMD -1.50, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.18, P = 0.03; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the incidence of deep venous thromboembolism between the CSF plus antibiotics group and the antibiotics-alone group (RR 1.68, 95% CI 0.72 to 3.93, P = 0.23; low-quality evidence). However, patients treated with CSFs were more likely to experience bone or joint pain and flu-like symptoms (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.42, P = 0.03; low-quality evidence). The overall methodological quality of the included studies ranged from moderate to low, with limitations primarily due to inconsistencies across studies and imprecise results. No full economic evaluations were identified, although some studies suggested potential economic benefits, such as reduced hospital length of stay, associated with the use of CSFs. However, these findings were insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about cost-effectiveness. In conclusion, the addition of CSFs to antibiotics in the treatment of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia did not improve overall mortality but was associated with shorter hospital stays, faster neutrophil recovery, shorter duration of neutropenia, quicker resolution of fever, and reduced duration of antibiotic use. The impact of CSFs on infection-related mortality remains unclear. Further research is needed to address the current gaps in evidence, particularly regarding the cost-effectiveness of this treatment approach.
